A1.text:
Russia and Ukraine report overnight attacks amid US diplomatic push
Overnight attacks reported on both sides as US efforts to broker a ceasefire struggle to make progress and Europe continues to ponder its role.
Russia and Ukraine have reported numerous overnight attacks, despite a diplomatic push to end the conflict.
Russian officials reported on Friday that a swarm of about 1,200 Ukrainian drones were fired at the country, with oil infrastructure among the targets. Ukraine reported that a hospital was struck and that strikes on the port of Odesa were ongoing.
The reports illustrate that hostilities continue unabated despite the renewed effort of United States envoys to mediate a ceasefire.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence reported it had intercepted 1,198 Ukrainian drones overnight, across more than 15 regions.
Attacks in Volgograd in southern Russia killed four people as they hit an industrial area and left two others injured, regional Governor Andrei Bocharov said.
Volgograd is home to a major oil refinery, which unverified video posted on social media purported to show was on fire. There was no immediate official confirmation that the refinery had been attacked.
Ukraine has concentrated its fire this year on Russia’s oil infrastructure in a bid to cut off its earnings from energy exports, which are being used to power its ongoing invasion.
Sergei Sobyanin, mayor of Moscow, said 467 Ukrainian drones had hit the capital overnight, according to the RIA Novosti news agency.
Ukraine reported that Russian forces had been attacking the southern port city of Odesa since early on Friday morning. The city’s military administration reported that at least two people had been killed.
The Russian Defence Ministry said it had targeted a cargo ship in the Black Sea that was transporting weapons and military equipment for Ukrainian forces, according to the TASS news agency.
Ukrainian emergency officials reported six people injured in Russian attacks in the southeastern Zaporizhia district.
A hospital in Kyiv caught fire overnight after being struck during a Russian drone attack, leaving one person injured.
Diplomatic push
The attacks came amid the renewed diplomatic push by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.
Russian and Ukrainian negotiators met in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday and Wednesday, reporting agreement on a major prisoner exchange but no progress towards ending the war.
Territory and security guarantees remain crucial obstacles. Russia is reported to have repeated uncompromising demands, including its right to control the entirety of Ukraine’s Donbas region.
Unconfirmed reports also said it had made demands regarding wider European security, including calling for Finland to leave NATO and for the Western military alliance to pledge not to base troops in the Baltic region.
The US diplomats met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday, then briefed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Dublin, before an informal meeting of European Union heads of state or government in the Irish capital on Friday.
Kushner said Putin has agreed to include Europe in the negotiations, although the Kremlin has not confirmed the claim. “We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table,” the US envoy said.
“I think it is self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in Dublin.
However, Europe continues to struggle on its approach, with disagreement over naming a lead negotiator before an expected return to talks between Russia and Ukraine next week.

A11.text:
The Gulf must build security that can outlast this war
Trump’s latest statement should accelerate the region’s move towards a layered and networked security architecture.
On November 10, Gulf defence ministers approved the establishment of a forward command in Kuwait under the Gulf Cooperation Council’s Unified Military Command, with forces to be allocated to it. The decision marks another step towards Gulf states taking greater collective responsibility for their security.
One day earlier, after meeting Qatar’s prime minister, US President Donald Trump had said: “Iran militarily is effectively over.” He also said the US blockade would continue and left open further military action. His remarks fell short of announcing an agreed end to the war.
Any opening for diplomacy deserves support. But even a lasting agreement would leave the Gulf’s underlying security problems unresolved. The Kuwait command’s value will depend on implementation and on how it connects with the region’s other security partnerships.
The answer requires abandoning the expectation that one grand security arrangement can resolve every threat facing the region. That expectation assumes a degree of agreement about enemies, priorities and acceptable risks that does not exist.
Iran’s attacks on Gulf states during this war, together with Israel’s September 2025 strike on Qatar, demonstrate the breadth of the challenge. A security architecture designed around only one adversary will leave serious gaps. Armed militias and terrorist groups add other risks, alongside cyberattacks, maritime disruption and the consequences of state failure in the neighbourhood. The erosion of international restraints on the use of force makes all of these problems harder to manage.
The most credible response to this complex set of threats is a security architecture that is both layered and networked. Gulf states are already moving in this direction. The task now is to make those arrangements work together and sustain the effort when the immediate pressure of war recedes.
Layering starts with the recognition that different partnerships do different jobs. National capabilities and cooperation within the Gulf Cooperation Council provide the foundation. The relationship with the United States remains central, while additional arrangements address needs that a single partner cannot meet.
Cooperation with US Central Command supplies an operational layer. The air and missile defence coordination cell opened at Al Udeid in January, for example, was designed to improve regional coordination, share threat warnings and prepare for contingencies.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed in August by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan, adds a collective defence commitment among its members. The Badr memorandum, signed in October by Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia, sets out cooperation in defence manufacturing, research and technical training.
These arrangements should be judged by the gaps they fill. Collective defence, operational coordination and industrial capacity reinforce one another, but none can substitute for the others. Buying an interceptor, producing its components and deciding who will use it in a crisis are separate problems.
The next step is to connect these layers so that capabilities developed through one partnership strengthen what countries can do through another. This is what makes the architecture networked.
Qatar offers a useful example. It shares GCC membership with Saudi Arabia and participates in Badr alongside Turkiye and Pakistan. It therefore connects to all three Mecca signatories through other arrangements, despite not being a party to Mecca itself.
Those connections create opportunities. Stronger production capacity or better coordination among shared partners could improve the capabilities available to Qatar through its own relationships. A more effective deterrent against attacks on a neighbour could also improve the wider security environment.

A127.text:
Folgen der Midterm-Niederlage Trump weist Vance zurecht – Vizepräsident soll sich auf die USA konzentrieren statt auf Iran
Nach der Midterm-Niederlage der Republikaner ging US-Vizepräsident JD Vance mit einem Posting auf X auf Distanz zu Donald Trump – nun hat sich der US-Präsident offenbar revanchiert: Vance solle seine vollständige und uneingeschränkte Aufmerksamkeit lieber auf die Kriminalität und Korruption in demokratisch regierten US-Städten richten als auf Iran, schrieb Trump auf seiner Plattform »Truth Social«.
»Wir brauchen kein Abkommen mit Iran. Diese Zeiten sind längst vorbei. Wir haben ihr Geld, Hunderte Milliarden Dollar, und wir haben ihre Meerenge!«, so Trump.
Durch den Fokus auf US-Städte könne mehr Geld eingespart werden als durch ein Abkommen mit Iran. »Unser Haushalt könnte durch die Unterbindung dieser kriminellen Aktivitäten im großen Stil schnell ausgeglichen werden. Korruption liegt der Führung der Demokraten im Blut!«, erklärte der Präsident, wohl wissend, dass viele prominente US-Demokraten im Midterm-Wahlkampf vor allem ihm selbst schamlose Korruption vorwarfen.
An Iran grenzt die Straße von Hormus, eine der weltweit wichtigsten Strecken für den Transport von Öl und Gas. Sie ist seit dem Beginn des Irankriegs weitgehend blockiert. Offenbar bezog sich Trump mit seinem Beitrag auf einen Artikel des »Wall Street Journal«, demzufolge Vance direkte Verhandlungen mit Iran erwägt.
Vance hatte den Irankrieg mitverantwortlich für die schwere Schlappe der Republikaner bei den Zwischenwahlen Anfang November gemacht. »Der Grund für unsere Niederlage ist der Krieg«, hatte Vance auf der Social-Media-Plattform X geschrieben. Zudem hatte er sich zuletzt um die Aufnahme von Gesprächen mit Iran bemüht. Die Demokraten hatten bei den Wahlen Anfang des Monats die Kontrolle über beide Kammern des Kongresses gewonnen.
Die Republikaner rüsten sich für die Zeit nach Trump. MAGA-Extremisten und Traditionalisten gehen gleichzeitig auf den Präsidenten los. Und seine potenziellen Kronprinzen lauern auf ihre Chance. Berichte über getöteten Militär Ukraine greift erneut Ziele in Russland an
Die Ukraine hat offenbar erneut Ziele in und um Sankt Petersburg angegriffen. Das finnische Militär berichtet, man habe einen nicht näher bestimmten »Angriff« auf ein russisches Kriegsschiff in der Ostsee registriert. Estnische Medien berichten von Schäden an einem kleineren Schiff der russischen Marine. Es sei später nach Sankt Petersburg zurückgekehrt. Ukrainische Medien berichteten , das Militär habe eine russische Korvette der Bujan-Klasse getroffen.
Laut finnischen Berichten ereignete sich der Angriff 40 bis 60 Kilometer vor der Küste des Nato-Landes im finnischen Meerbusen. Nach Angaben von Markku Viitasaari, dem Direktor der Nationalen Verteidigungseinheit Finnlands, befand sich das russische Schiff vermutlich in der Region, um die russische Schattenflotte zu schützen. Bereits am frühen Mittwochmorgen war eine Drohne auch im finnischen Luftraum gesichtet worden. Der Luftraum um Helsinki wurde daraufhin zeitweilig gesperrt. Viitasaari sagte dem SPIEGEL und anderen Medien in Helsinki, es sei der dritte derartige Vorfall bislang gewesen.
Woher die Drohne stammte, konnte zunächst nicht abschließend geklärt werden. Nach bisherigen Erfahrungen dürfte sie jedoch aus der Ukraine gekommen und womöglich fehlgeleitet worden sein. Nach dem jetzigen Vorfall betonte der Brigadegeneral, dass sich der Angriff in internationalen Gewässern ereignet habe.
Erneut Militärangehöriger in Auto getötet
Unterdessen griff die Ukraine womöglich auch auf dem Festland weitere Ziele an. Bei der Explosion eines Autos in Sankt Petersburg wurde den Behörden zufolge ein Angehöriger des russischen Militärs getötet. Der Mann sei ums Leben gekommen, als das von ihm gesteuerte Auto gesprengt wurde, teilten die Ermittlungsbehörden mit. Es sei ein Strafverfahren wegen Mordes an einem Angehörigen der Streitkräfte eingeleitet worden.
Der Vorfall ereignete sich demnach im Stadtbezirk Puschkinski. Sankt Petersburg ist Russlands zweitgrößte Stadt. Der Militärangehörige wurde zunächst nicht identifiziert. Die lokale Onlinezeitung »Fontanka« berichtete jedoch, der Getötete habe den Rang eines Obersts gehabt. Dies konnte bislang noch nicht unabhängig bestätigt werden.
Zerstörtes Fahrzeug in Sankt Petersburg
Foto: Andrei Bok / REUTERS
Videoaufnahmen zeigten Absperrungen der Militärpolizei sowie Ermittler und Forensiker bei der Arbeit am Tatort. Ein durch die Bombe beschädigter dunkelblauer SUV stand mit geöffneten Türen, offener Motorhaube und offenem Kofferraum auf einer mit Trümmerteilen übersäten Straße. Daneben war ein ebenfalls beschädigter Bus zu sehen.
Eine Stellungnahme aus der Ukraine lag zunächst nicht vor. Russland hat die Ukraine in der Vergangenheit für tödliche Anschläge auf hochrangige Militärvertreter und Personen verantwortlich gemacht. Ende August war ein Militärangehöriger bei einer Autoexplosion im selben Bezirk von Sankt Petersburg getötet worden. Ähnliche Anschläge gab es in den vergangenen Monaten auch in Moskau sowie auf der Krim.
Putin bekräftigt Besitzansprüche
Bei den Gesprächen der beiden US-Unterhändler Steve Witkoff und Jared Kushner in Moskau zeichnet sich bislang dagegen kein Durchbruch ab. Staatschef Wladimir Putin bekräftigte vielmehr die russischen Gebietsforderungen an die Ukraine. Im Gespräch sagte der Kremlchef, für Russland gebe es nur eine mögliche Grenzlinie zur Ukraine, und das sei die offizielle russische Außengrenze. Diese Grenze umfasst nach Putins Verständnis auch ukrainische Gebiete, die Russland annektiert hat. Vom Gesprächsauftakt veröffentlichte der Kreml einen Videomitschnitt.
Später hieß es, Putin schlage eine sogenannte humanitäre Mission für die ukrainische Stadt Kostjantyniwka vor. Man könne dort »das Gleiche tun« wie in Oleschky, so Putin. In der ebenfalls umkämpften Stadt hatte Russland zunächst die Bevölkerung wochenlang mit seinem Militär ausgehungert und dann nach Verhandlungen Hunderten Zivilisten die Ausreise ermöglicht.

A207.text:
Rebel attacks are killing health care workers and destroying clinics in the Ebola zone in Congo, jeopardizing efforts to fight the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak in history, humanitarian agencies say.
The insurgent violence is the latest blow to an Ebola response that often struggles with a lack of basic supplies − including phones, fuel and water − according to health care workers in eastern regions of the DRC.
In just six months, the epidemic has now infected more than 11,100 people, killing more than 5,430 of them. The outbreak has become the second-biggest in history, but it is expanding much faster than the deadliest Ebola epidemic, which killed more than 11,300 people in West Africa from 2014 to 2016.
Despite the negative trends, there are early signs that a Canadian-developed vaccine designed for a different Ebola virus could be effective against the Bundibugyo Ebola virus that is rampant in eastern Congo, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said this week.
Congo rolls out Canadian-developed vaccine to fight Ebola outbreak
Islamist rebels launched violent assaults in Congo’s Ebola zone last week, killing 66 civilians, including three health workers, and destroying three clinics in the town of Cantine-Aloya.
Attacks have continued since then, including as recently as Wednesday night, causing panic among local people, disrupting health operations and scattering Ebola-exposed people across a wide area, World Health Organization officials say.
Workers are still searching for those who fled the attacks last week, including three confirmed Ebola patients and more than 1,000 contacts of people with the virus, the WHO officials said at a briefing Thursday.
“We need an urgent halt in hostilities and violence,” said Marie Belizaire, a regional emergency director for the WHO. “Continued violence risks reversing the progress made over the past six months, putting more lives at risk and allowing transmission to continue.”
WHO director-general Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the rising insecurity in eastern Congo is now one of the greatest obstacles to the Ebola response. But rebel attacks are far from the only threat to workers at a time of community distrust and hostility.
A nurse was killed and another health worker badly injured when responding to an Ebola alert last month, Dr. Tedros said. Other attacks have included arson attempts, a grenade left near a health office, gunfire near a treatment centre and stone-throwing incidents.
“These incidents restrict humanitarian access, disrupt operations, make it harder to reach communities quickly, and give the virus an advantage,” he said.
While WHO officials have repeatedly insisted that progress is being made, the Ebola outbreak “remains out of control” and basic resources are still lacking in the often dysfunctional response, MSF said in a downbeat report Thursday.
Hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent on the response, but front-line health workers are stuck with “empty hands and empty pockets,” MSF international president Javid Abdelmoneim said in the report.
“Our teams are often left speechless by the dysfunctions they witness in many areas. Six months into the response, this situation is simply unacceptable.”
Among the problems he cited were a lack of training and wages for health workers, a shortage of fuel for ambulances, community workers without phones or mobile data, surveillance teams that exist only on paper, persistent shortages of personal protective equipment and health facilities operating without adequate water and chlorine. “This has turned some facilities into new centres of transmission,” Dr. Abdelmoneim said.
Opinion: Surveillance alone won’t prevent the next Ebola epidemic
Surveillance efforts are aimed at identifying Ebola cases in the community – but instead, more than 90 per cent of patients are identified only when they turn up sick at a health facility, and almost two-thirds are dying before they reach a clinic, he said.

A215.text:
Spain’s interim lower house of parliament on Thursday ratified housing measures designed to limit evictions and real estate speculation, a day after a general strike and major street protests over the country’s housing cost crunch.
The duration of the approved measures, however, will likely depend on the outcome of a national election set for later this month.
The leading opposition party, the conservative Popular Party, has said that it will repeal the housing measures of the left wing government if it takes power, which polls indicate is a real possibility.
“Yesterday, the right to housing won on the street and in workplaces, and I hope it will win again at the ballot box,” interim housing minister Isabel Rodríguez told lawmakers, in reference to Wednesday’s general strike and the upcoming election on Nov. 29.
Spain’s government had tried to push through the measures in October after public anger over soaring rents erupted following the nationally televised eviction and subsequent death of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid.
Workers across Spain stage first general strike in 14 years over housing crisis
But the PP and other conservative parties aligned in parliament to reject the measures. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez responded days later by calling an early election.
The government then waited to try again to pass the measures with a smaller interim parliament, where it and aligned progressive parties had a slightly more favorable distribution of seats.
The government split the measures into two decrees, with one measure that appeared doomed from the start being separated into a second decree so as not to put the rest in danger.
The first decree containing a package of measures succeeded in passing on Thursday, while the second decree was, as expected, rejected again.
Measures to help tenants
The interim lower house has 69 members, compared with 350 in the regular parliament, which was dissolved when the election was called.
The first decree passed in a 35-34 vote.
The decree that passed included a measure that extends protections against evictions for tenants deemed by social services to be in a precarious financial or social position as long as regional authorities can’t offer them an alternative residence. The measure will last until 2030.
Another main feature is an attempt to reduce real estate speculation by impeding any company involved in the real estate market from buying properties for less than 70 per cent of their value. That is meant to stop wholesale purchase of properties at low prices, and their subsequent resale at higher prices.
Millions of Spaniards demand housing reform during nationwide strike
The decree also stops rent increases for rents that already exceed the reference price established by the government’s index of prices for that given neighborhood.
It also establishes a 10-per-cent tax on apartments rented to tourists – like those on online platforms such as Airbnb, which have become a target of public scorn – along with a tax incentive to encourage leasing and government-backed loans for down payments on homes for residential use.
Lawmakers again reject indefinite leases
The second decree, which was once again rejected, would have made residential leases automatically renewable by tenants. If owners wanted to break contracts, they would have had to compensate tenants with a year’s worth of rent.
Many lawmakers deemed that measure would have led homeowners to withdraw properties from the rental market, triggering a drop in supply and even higher prices. It was rejected 34-35 after a centre-right Basque party voted with the right-wing bloc after having supported the other decree.
“You promised us more housing and have only given us tons of demagoguery,” PP lawmaker Sergio Sayas told the minister.
The PP has pledged to oversee the construction of one million new homes while slashing taxes and red tape for real estate development if they return to power after eight years of Socialist-led rule.

A216.text:
An American Army officer who was arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion of spying for Russia had not handed over any information to Moscow and he is expected to be charged in Britain in the coming days, a U.S. official said Thursday.
After the British charges are filed against Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, expected on Sunday or Monday, the intention is then to prosecute him under the U.S. military justice system, the official said. No information made it into Russian hands, the official said.
A second U.S. official also confirmed Tyner’s name and said he had been previously deployed to Afghanistan, Iraq and Qatar. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.
Tyner was a senior human resources officer and had been assigned to a NATO unit at a base near Gloucester, England. He was arrested Tuesday on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information.
The Metropolitan Police announced the arrest this week and said its counterterror forces worked closely with the FBI and U.S. military.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov denied that Russia has any connection to the U.S. officer.
“This arrest does not concern us in any way. We don’t know what it’s connected to,” Peskov told journalists on Wednesday, according to Russian news services. “We have nothing to do with this and it has nothing to do with us.”
Tyner was serving in NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester. The multinational land unit within the NATO military alliance is designed to quickly respond to crises or short-notice operations. According to the unit’s website, it is made up of forces from 20 nations but is led by the British.
Police said the arrest was not related to other counterterrorism investigations, indicating no connection with a suspected terror plot linked to Iran in September at a U.S.-run base in Britain, RAF Fairford, near Gloucester.

A229.text:
World leaders have set out competing positions and made clashing demands in two days of intense speech-making at the COP31 climate change talks in Turkey, leaving negotiators with a tough task to draft a meaningful deal that all can agree.
Small island states, among the most vulnerable in the world as global warming makes sea levels rise, pleaded for urgent cuts to greenhouse gas emissions.
European leaders, meanwhile, lined up behind a proposal to expand global electrification, developing countries asked for more finance from rich ones, and fossil fuel producers said oil, gas, and coal should continue to be used.
“We reaffirm our sovereign right to strengthen our energy and oil industry as a driver of our national development,” Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodriguez told the conference, after UN leaders had made the case for bringing to an end the age of fossil fuel.
War and conflict must not distract from fight against global warming, leaders warn COP31
Apart from trying to accommodate incompatible national positions aired on Wednesday and Thursday, conference host Turkey and negotiations lead Australia also have the challenge of trying to make progress when wars and inflation have pushed climate concerns down the political agenda.
“It’s my job to steer consensus, not to bang tables and demand any particular action, but to steer consensus to the strongest, most ambitious possible outcome within the constraints of that consensus-driven process,” Chris Bowen, Australia’s COP31 president of negotiations, told Reuters.
Asked what a good deal might look like, he said: “I have many more hours of consultations with partners to do.”
Climate activists say short-term political concerns should not get in the way of addressing an issue that will get more pressing if ignored.
UN sees higher global warming even if countries reduce heat-trapping emissions
A UN report last month found the world was already on course to break through the 1.5 degrees Celsius warming limit that countries had agreed to pursue under the 2015 Paris Agreement to prevent the worst effects of climate change.
“The situation could not be less under control. The planet is not dying. It is being killed,” Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg said on the sidelines of the UN conference.
“It is being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue. No one is coming to our rescue.”
Britain’s Burnham backs renewables
Earlier on Thursday, the leaders of small island states including the Bahamas, Tuvalu, the Solomon Islands and Saint Lucia called for swift action.
“Major emitters must move beyond the usual promises. They must reduce emissions that the climate crisis demands,” said Saint Lucia’s Prime Minister Philip J. Pierre.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham backed a proposal by Turkey to increase electricity’s share of world energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035, from a little over a fifth now, to help advance that goal. Turkey has not specified whether the extra energy used would be renewable.
Burnham told the conference that energy supply disruptions from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and Russia’s war with Ukraine showed clean energy was the wise choice.
Turtles offer early warning to how climate change is altering ecosystems ahead of COP31
“It is now plain for everyone to see that if we depend on energy we do not control, then we leave ourselves exposed to prices we cannot control,” he said. “The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security.”
Developing countries reiterated requests that they have made during many years of UN talks for rich countries to provide more finance to help them shift to cleaner energy, adapt to a warming world, and repair climate-driven destruction.

A25.text:
Iran says it targeted US radar site in Bahrain
IRGC claims Bahrain radar strike is a response to attacks on Iranian telecom tower in southern Hormozgan province.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has targeted a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for what it described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran.
The claim came hours after Iran’s state news agency IRNA, citing official sources, reported that the port city of Sirik in Hormozgan province was hit by “enemy fire” on Thursday.
In a statement carried by the semi-official Tasnim news agency, the IRGC called the strike a “serious warning” to the “aggressor enemy” to stop what it said was a series of aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz.
“Should these violations and acts of aggression recur, the IRGC Aerospace Force stands in full readiness to engage without limits,” the statement said.
The IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said the IRGC’s Aerospace Force had “targeted and destroyed” the radar installation.
There was no immediate comment from Washington or Manama.
Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet.
The Fifth Fleet headquarters, at the Naval Support Activity base in the capital, Manama, is the main command centre for US naval operations in the Middle East.
It was hit in the opening hours of the war on February 28, and satellite images analysed by Al Jazeera showed direct hits on several radar domes and damage to buildings across the base.
The US has reportedly reduced its troop numbers at bases in the region and ordered some diplomatic staff to leave, according to news outlets, as Trump weighs new strikes on Iran,
US Central Command said it “regularly” moves personnel and assets to “optimise mission readiness”.
First Bahrain attack since September
According to the Reuters news agency, it is the first time since early September that Iran has claimed an attack on US military assets in a Gulf country.
The claim comes as Israel’s security cabinet has ordered the military to step up preparations for a possible attack on Iran, according to Israeli media, including the public broadcaster KAN.
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei has warned that if the US launches another war, every military base involved, anywhere from West Asia to Europe, would be a legitimate target for Iranian strikes.
A Pentagon inspector general’s report released in September found that Iranian attacks damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings at US installations in eight countries, including Bahrain, in the first four months of the war.
Analysts say several US bases in the region have been almost rendered unusable.
US President Donald Trump has said he is prepared to return to war if the diplomatic track offered by Qatar fails to deliver a deal.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, has said economic pressure on Iran is working well enough that resuming large-scale military operations is unnecessary.
In an exclusive interview with Al Jazeera on Wednesday, Iran’s parliament speaker and lead negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Strait of Hormuz would never go back to how it was before the war, and that “the ball is now in the American court“.
Meanwhile, US Central Command says its forces are still strictly enforcing the naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The war began on February 28 with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.

A28.text:
Iran's Guards say they targeted a US early-warning radar in Bahrain
Nov 13 (Reuters) - Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Friday they targeted a US early-warning radar in Bahrain, the first such claim of an attack on American military assets in a Gulf country since early September.
The Guards said the strike was in retaliation for what they described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in Iran's southern Sirik county, in Hormozgan province, according to Iranian state media.
The claim came amid a fragile lull in the conflict between Iran and the US, which began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28 and has since spread across the region.
Iran launched missile and drone attacks on US bases in Gulf states and sought to restrict shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global oil and gas supplies. Washington, in turn, imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
There was no immediate comment from the US or Bahrain.
(Reporting by Hatem Maher; Editing by Muralikumar Anantharaman and Thomas Derpinghaus)

So many people are dying of Ebola that their bodies have been stacked, one atop the other, on makeshift racks in a shed by the hospital gate.
The town’s main cemetery is full, so fresh graves are being squeezed in between palm trees by the side of the road.
Medicine, IVs and basic protections have been so scarce that three-quarters of Ebola patients in this besieged Congolese town have died.
Supported by
Caught Between Killers: Ebola on One Side, Islamic State on the Other
Six months on, Ebola continues to hack a deadly trail across eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
When the outbreak was first detected in May, it resembled a single, giant blaze, with infections concentrated in a handful of towns in one province.
It has since morphed into a far bigger, more elusive foe, creeping into eight provinces and splintering into numerous hot spots as its moves through one of the world’s great rainforests.
Instead of one big fire, there are many now, scattered across a vast area about the size of Britain.
Health workers have corralled the virus where it was first detected, but infections are soaring elsewhere. Biakato, a small town deep in the rainforest, suddenly accounted for as many as one-quarter of new cases nationally. Yet its beleaguered residents were left almost entirely on their own, with dangerously little to defend themselves against the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
“We see the same mistakes as before,” said Dr. Jean-Jacques Muyembe, who helped discover Ebola in 1976 and now heads Congo’s National Institute for Biomedical Research. “It’s as if we were starting from zero. It’s very disappointing.”
And if that were not enough, the campaign to contain the epidemic has run into a terrifying new threat: the Islamic State.

Democratic control of Congress could quickly lead to sanctions on violent Israeli settlers and on new settlement construction in the occupied West Bank, as well as to new conditions on arms sales.

Army Officer Accused of Trying to Spy for Russia Is Afghan War Veteran
The officer, who served at a NATO base in Britain, is expected to be charged in the coming days, two officials said.
A U.S. Army officer arrested in Britain on suspicion of trying to spy for Russia is a decorated veteran of the Afghanistan war who was caught in a sting operation, according to two American officials familiar with the case.
The suspect, Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, was arrested this week. British officials are expected to charge him on Sunday or Monday, and after that, the U.S. Army will seek to charge him under the Uniform Code of Military Justice and transfer him to the United States, the two officials said. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing inquiry.
Beyond the sting, it was not clear what actions prompted Colonel Tyner’s arrest. He was based at the headquarters of NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps in Gloucestershire, about 100 miles west of London. The base is NATO’s largest in Britain and hosts troops from 20 allied nations responsible for rapid response to crises.
In a statement announcing the arrest, the F.B.I. director, Kash Patel, said the case involved “allegations of espionage.” Though officials said in a statement that “the country to which the allegations relate is Russia,” it is unclear whether Colonel Tyner actually handed over sensitive information to Moscow.
Cellphone numbers for Colonel Tyner and his wife were disconnected. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier that he had been caught in a sting.
The Kremlin has denied any involvement. “This arrest has nothing to do with us, and we don’t know what it is connected to,” the Kremlin’s spokesman, Dmitri S. Peskov, said at a news conference on Wednesday.
Colonel Tyner has been enlisted as a senior human resources officer in the Army since January 2008 and was deployed to Afghanistan for a year starting in December 2013. He also served in Iraq in 2019 and 2020 and Qatar before that. He is the recipient of a Bronze Star Medal and the Defense Meritorious Service Medal, among other awards.
His LinkedIn page indicates that he received a bachelor’s degree in criminology from the University of North Carolina at Pembroke.
In Britain, counterterrorism police have investigated several high-profile terrorism cases related to the United States in the past months, including two cases of arrests near air bases in England where the American military operates.
On Tuesday, federal prosecutors in the United States said that the commander of a powerful Iranian-backed militia helped direct a plot while sitting in a Brooklyn prison against R.A.F. Fairford, a military airfield used by American bombers in the war against Iran. In September, five men were arrested and then later released on bail near the base in connection with the plot.
Separately, two Latvian men were arrested in October on suspicion of a national security offense after breaching the perimeter of R.A.F. Molesworth, about 70 miles north of London, in Cambridgeshire, England.
British police said the arrest of Colonel Tyner was not related to those cases.
Michael Schwirtz is the global intelligence correspondent for The Times based in London.
Eric Schmitt is a national security correspondent for The Times. He has reported on U.S. military affairs and counterterrorism for more than three decades. Contact him securely on Signal: @ericschmitt.36.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden resignation amid an explosive espionage scandal has thrown the future of the world’s most valuable chipmaker into uncertainty. For the Middle East, where Nvidia investments and access to the company’s chips have become key to government technology ambitions, the fallout could have significant consequences.
What happened: Huang resigned Thursday after revelations about two extramarital affairs emerged, ending his reign at the company he co-founded in 1993 and turned into the world's leading supplier of the chips fueling the artificial intelligence boom. His infidelities included one with a suspected Chinese spy and another with a company employee. Nvidia's board appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim leader, leaving the roughly $4 trillion chipmaker facing an uncertain succession.
The scandal has already raised far-reaching questions about national security and Huang's judgment, particularly given his position at the center of the global AI industry and his extensive contacts with political leaders. President Donald Trump, who developed a close relationship with Huang in the past two years, publicly stood by the embattled CEO earlier this week, saying he believed Huang was unaware of the alleged espionage links despite reports indicating the White House had been briefed.
In the hours before Huang's ouster, prominent voices from the Gulf had come to his defense. Saudi investor Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed posted on X on Wednesday that "if Nvidia board fires Jensen Huang, that would be the dumbest thing they've ever done." Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
- Published
Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.
Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.
The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.
Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.
Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.
The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.
Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.
Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.
Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."
The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.
"The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.
Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.
Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.
Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace.
He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.
Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.
Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

Uno de los dos decretos sobre vivienda que el presidente Pedro Sánchez apuró para desinflamar los reclamos de los inquilinos en España y que desencadenaron el adelanto electoral que él mismo anunció para el 29 de noviembre obtuvo finalmente este jueves la convalidación parlamentaria indispensable para que sus medidas se concreten.
Fue la Diputación Permanente, la representación legislativa que se activa en los períodos preelectorales una vez que se disuelven las Cortes Generales, la que esta vez consiguió los votos favorables suficientes para lograr la suspensión de los desalojos y la prórroga por dos años de los contratos de alquiler que venzan antes de 2029.
Esta vez fue posible porque la Diputación Permanente es una representación reducida de los grupos parlamentarios con una aritmética propia que, sumando el voto de la presidente del Congreso, favoreció a la propuesta del gobierno.
La convalidación de las medidas llegan horas después de la primera huelga general que vivió España en 14 años y que tuvo su germen en las demandas de vivienda y salarios dignos para poder pagarla.
El decreto Maricarmen
Eran dos los reales decretos que el gobierno había aprobado luego del desgarrador desalojo de Maricarmen Abascal, que se convirtió en símbolo de las penurias de los inquilinos.
Maricarmen era una vecina de 87 años y en silla de ruedas que fue echada del departamento que su familia alquiló durante siete décadas porque así se lo exigía el fondo de inversión inmobiliaria que lo había comprado. Maricarmen murió dos semanas después en un hospital.
En en decreto que este jueves finalmente fue aprobado, el gobierno de Sánchez proponía, además de la renovación de los contratos por dos años, beneficios fiscales para los propietarios que saquen al mercado del alquiler sus propiedades a precio asequible, limitar la compra de casas y departamentos por parte de fondos buitre hasta 2030 y suspender los desalojos de personas vulnerables si el propietario es una empresa dueña de varias propiedades.
El segundo real decreto ley, propuesto por Sumar -el socio minoritario en la coalición de gobierno progresista que lidera el PSOE-, postulaba la prórroga indefinida de los contratos de alquiler, decreto que fue rechazo por el Parlamento ordinario, antes de que Sánchez lo disolviera, y por la Diputación Permanente que sesiona en las vísperas electorales cuando no hay Congreso.
Antes del inicio de la campaña electoral
La convalidación del real decreto ley que el gobierno había aprobado llegó horas después de la huelga general motivada por la crisis de la vivienda.
Y un día antes del inicio de la campaña electoral para las elecciones anticipadas que Sánchez convocó después de que el Parlamento le bochara los decretos de vivienda en octubre.
Con las calles tomadas por la protesta social de los inquilinos que desembocó en la huelga general del miércoles 11 y hasta una acampada en la Puerta del Sol que duró un mes y se replicó en varias ciudades española, Sánchez vio un hueco favorable para el adelanto electoral que la oposición llevaba tiempo reclamándole.
Cargaba con la mochila de las investigaciones judiciales y los casos de corrupción en el PSOE, la gestión de la crisis migratoria en Ceuta y las dudas sobre la seguridad ferroviaria, a pesar de que aún no se había producido el último choque de trenes de Toledo.
Y creyó ver una luz a su favor en la negativa de la derecha a aprobar los decretos que aliviaban la angustia de los inquilinos.
El “no” del PP, Vox y Junts
El Partido Popular (PP), Vox y Junts per Catalunya -la fuerza independentista conservadora del ex presidente catalán Carles Puigdemont- votaron en contra de los decretos, en octubre y este jueves, en la Diputación Permanente.

Small island states, among the most vulnerable in the world as global warming makes sea levels rise, pleaded for urgent cuts to greenhouse gas emissions.
European leaders, meanwhile, lined up behind a proposal to expand global electrification, developing countries asked for more finance from rich ones, and fossil fuel producers said oil, gas, and coal should continue to be used.

Climate activists say short-term political concerns should not get in the way of addressing an issue that will get more pressing if ignored.
A UN report last month found the world was already on course to break through the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming limit that countries had agreed to pursue under the 2015 Paris Agreement to prevent the worst effects of climate change.
"The situation could not be less under control. The planet is not dying. It is being killed," Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg said on the sidelines of the UN conference.
"It is being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue. No one is coming to our rescue."
BRITAIN'S BURNHAM BACKS RENEWABLES
Earlier on Thursday, the leaders of small island states including the Bahamas, Tuvalu, the Solomon Islands and Saint Lucia called for swift action.
"Major emitters must move beyond the usual promises. They must reduce emissions that the climate crisis demands," said Saint Lucia's Prime Minister Philip J. Pierre.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham backed a proposal by Turkey to increase electricity's share of world energy consumption to 35% by 2035, from a little over a fifth now, to help advance that goal. Turkey has not specified whether the extra energy used would be renewable.
Burnham told the conference that energy supply disruptions from the US-Israeli war with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine showed clean energy was the wise choice.
"It is now plain for everyone to see that if we depend on energy we do not control, then we leave ourselves exposed to prices we cannot control," he said. "The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security."
Developing countries reiterated requests that they have made during many years of UN talks for rich countries to provide more finance to help them shift to cleaner energy, adapt to a warming world, and repair climate-driven destruction.
Fernanda de Carvalho, the head of climate policy for the World Wildlife Fund environmental group, said she found the leaders' speeches underwhelming, especially as COP31 is the first UN conference since scientists have publicly said the world is set to breach the 1.5C threshold.
"It is worrying that the climate issue is not as high on the global political agenda as it needs to be," she said.
(Reporting by William James, Valerie Volcovici, Simon Jessop, and Tuvan Gumrukcu; Writing by Richard Valdmanis; editing by Barbara Lewis)

A137.text:
EU leaders tussle over whom to send to Ukraine, Russia peace talks
November 12, 2026
European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.
When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.
The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi, followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy.
Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.
Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine, alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz insisted Europe will be present.
"At the table must be sitting Ukraine, must be sitting the Europeans, must be sitting the Americans, and naturally Russia," he told reporters in Dublin.
But he, like many other leaders, played down the idea of appointing a special envoy for the talks.
A divided Europe
Zelenskyy is insistent on European involvement in the peace talks.
"Not directly yet, and not yet when the Russians are at the table," he told the other leaders during the Dublin meetings. "But Europeans are already involved. And we need to make sure that Europe becomes a regular part of these negotiations."
Europe’s division over exactly who should be present has caused a public battle to erupt. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote an excoriating letter to Costa last week, bemoaning the lack of unity.
"By projecting the image of a Europe that is in disarray, we are merely serving the interests of those who want this war to continue," wrote Meloni.
European leaders had even seemed divided over their level of frustration about the situation.
Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Jansa said in Dublin that it was creating a "bad mood" among leaders, however Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs disputed those comments saying, "I don’t feel that."
European security at stake
The palpable fear among the leaders in Dublin is that the US will accept Russia's demands that Europe changes the way it structures its own security, mainly through the NATO military alliance, in exchange for a seat at the table.
Putin said a commitment that Ukraine will never join NATO and even the potential rolling back of the alliance to remove new joiners Finland and Sweden, could be among his demands.
"What do we hear from them [Europeans]?" asked Putin during the meeting with Kushner and Witkoff in Moscow. "That once a peace agreement is signed, they will immediately deploy troops in Ukraine. This is a legitimate target for us, so the war will resume immediately."
This is exactly the kind of rhetoric the European leaders say they are most wary of, especially those in Russia’s direct neighborhood.
"Right now, we are in the [Russian] trap," said Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal.

Climate Forward
Leaders at COP31 are confronting a new reality as global warming enters the “unsafe zone.”
It was the climate movement’s unifying slogan for the past decade: “Keep 1.5 Alive.”
The tagline referred to the central ambition of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, in which almost every country pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.
Now, just 11 years after the target was set, 1.5 is effectively dead.
Scientists now say that without drastic efforts to reduce greenhouse gases, it is very likely that the planet will warm at least 2.6 degrees Celsius, or 4.7 degrees Fahrenheit, by the end of the century.
At COP31, the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, diplomats who spent so long championing the 1.5 degree target lamented the abrupt setback.
“The world has no chance of holding to 1.5 degrees,” said Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy, who is leading the negotiations.
Scientists for years have warned that allowing global average temperatures to rise 1.5 degrees Celsius, or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit, above preindustrial levels would result in a profoundly more dangerous world. Extreme heat will become more common and more intense. Storms will become more powerful and destructive. Sea levels will rise. And poor countries will bear the brunt of the damage.
That scenario is already playing out around the world. In recent months, wildfires have raged from Canada to Indonesia. The collapse of a glacier in Nepal killed thousands and wiped away towns. Floods and mudslides devastated Brazil. And a European heat wave killed an estimated 50,000 people.

As election nears, Spain's Sanchez struggles to rally disillusioned left
MADRID, Nov 13 - When Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a snap election last month, he was betting that anger over housing and fear of the far right would rally all shades of the left behind his Socialists.
But interviews and polls suggest that many potential supporters are too furious about the status quo and the perceived failings of his own incumbent government to oblige.
The eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in September, and her subsequent death, triggered protests against a housing crisis that culminated in a general strike which unions said brought more than 3 million on to the streets on Wednesday.
"Every generation has its own struggle — for us, that struggle is housing," Sanchez said at his first rally after calling the vote.
His challenge as he prepares to face the electorate on November 29 is that the protests led by movements even further to his left have moved well beyond accommodation.
'WE'RE REALLY TIRED OF SO MANY THINGS'
"We're really tired of so many things," said Maria Torrena Perez, a 40-year-old primary school teacher at a march in Madrid on Wednesday night.
"We need decent housing. We need a quality public education system. We need a decent healthcare system. Ultimately, they're not investing in what they should be investing in. And we're fed up with the policies being implemented across the board."
Two deadly train crashes, corruption convictions in Sanchez's inner circle and a rush of migrants into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta have all taken their toll on Sanchez's support.
For all his campaigning, polls show backing for his party is still hovering around the 26%-29% level recorded before he called the election.
Without a shift in the next two weeks, an alliance between the conservative People's Party and far-right Vox, a hardline nationalist party championing tighter borders and deregulation, is seen as the most likely next government.
Interviews with left-of-centre politicians, activists and voters suggested that for many, disillusionment with the status quo outweighs the urge to keep the far right out.
The "lesser evil" pitch of a centrist government standing between them and an ever-harder right is wearing thin, echoing discontent with incumbents that has spilled into social unrest across Europe in recent months.
Sanchez has branded the prospect of a PP-Vox government a threat to social rights won in recent decades, describing a coalition of the two parties in a recent campaign video as "two colours, one project of regression".
Some have turned that against him. Sanchez's "self-styled progressive government is a government of slower regression," said Mario Aguiriano, spokesperson for the Socialist Movement popular among students which gained prominence in Spain's protest encampments.
"Is the enemy who kills you slowly with poison preferable to the enemy who kills you with a chainsaw?"
Sanchez's Socialist Party "plays in elections and campaigns at being the Che Guevara of the left — but progressive voters aren't going to be fooled," Tesh Sidi, a lawmaker left of Sanchez, said as she explained why voters should choose her "Broad Front" party over their senior partners in the government coalition.
'VOTING ISN'T ENOUGH'
The breakdown of talks last month among Spain's left-of-centre parties to form a united platform means disgruntled leftist voters face a choice between sticking with the Socialists, abstaining, or voting for a smaller party that might end up letting the right in.
Many — emboldened by the scale and impact of street protests in Spain and across Europe, from Serbia to neighbouring Portugal — have suggested that electoral politics may no longer be the best way to get change.
"Voting isn't enough," said Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for the Tenants Union which called Wednesday's general strike.
It was vital not to "hand fascism a seat" but voting was just one way to make a difference.

Donald Trump has said that the US is no longer seeking a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered JD Vance, who had spearheaded recent efforts to restart negotiations with Iran, to focus on domestic politics instead.
In a post to his social media site on Thursday, Trump said he was redirecting the vice-president to focus his “complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S”.
Vance had reportedly been talking to intermediaries in Iran and Qatar about restarting negotiations to end the war, which began in February when the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran. Iran responded by closing access to the strait of Hormuz, which led to a steep increase for the cost of fuel around the globe.
But on Thursday Trump appeared to shut down the negotiations, redirecting Vance to focus on domestic issues and downplaying the need for a final deal.
“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”
The announcement effectively normalises a stalemate with Iran. The US has maintained a blockade on Iranian ports and mostly reopened the strait of Hormuz to marine traffic, including crude oil shipments. But the US has not carried out massive strikes against Iran for several months, and Iran has not launched barrages of ballistic missiles against US bases and allies in the region.
Trump last week also downplayed the possibility of new strikes on Iran and said that the war was “effectively over”.
During a White House press conference, Trump said that Israel and Gulf allies in the region were well protected from Iran, and that an escalation was not needed.
“At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing – but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” he told reporters during a briefing at the White House, which took place shortly after he met with Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani.
Trump said he had been lobbied by the leaders of Gulf states not to resume the war.
The decision effectively sidelines Vance from the main foreign policy challenge of his vice-presidency. He had publicly distanced himself from the war, and in April he led a US delegation to Islamabad to negotiate an end to it. Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff have also been involved in negotiations.
Axios last week reported that Vance was speaking “almost daily” with Sheikh Mohammed; Pakistan’s army head, Asim Munir; and other mediators. Several weeks ago he also sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, to resume direct negotiations.
Vance last week blamed the conflict for the historic rout dealt to Republicans in the midterm elections.
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said after the midterms in a lengthy post on X. “The president himself said so last night.”
Trump has since doubled down on launching the war on Iran, admitting that it drove up fuel prices but repeating his frequent assertion that it was needed to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

Europe should not 'walk into the traps that Russia is setting' on negotiating sequence, Kallas says
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has warned against the EU agreeing to Russia’s proposed sequence of talks on Ukraine, saying it would allow Moscow to “divert the attention away” from its actions and ultimately leave Europe “in a worse place.”
She welcomed the US side “finally admitting what I said already one and a half years ago – that for any deal between Russia and Ukraine … you also need the Europeans.”
“I hope that we are just not at the table, but we are actually also really influencing the outcome of these negotiations.”
She said:
“The most important is that we keep to our agreement that first the ceasefire, then peace agreement and then any kind of other talks … when Russia is still presenting their maximum demands, then we should also stick to the maximum demands and start to negotiate from there. …
Kallas warned that there is a risk of Europeans “actually walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as Moscow is trying to “divert the attention away from that there is no ceasefire and actually [get us to] start to listen to their claims.”
“If we walk into that trap that we start to discuss … the European security architecture, then I don’t think we are in a better place. We are actually in worse place.”
She continued:
“Let’s focus on what it is at hand. We have one aggressor and one victim. The aggressor does not have security concerns, as nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”
Kallas is also very clear that she wants to be part of the EU negotiating team, saying she was appointed to represent Europe on foreign and security policy.
“I know that the Russians don’t want me, but do we have a say on who is representing Russia? No, we don’t.”
She also said that ultimately she would not be “representing myself,” but bound by any mandate given to her by the 27.
Slightly amused/frustrated with repeated questions on what’s holding up the EU with deciding on its representation, she eventually hits back with this line:
“Well, we have institutions in place, so we can’t just send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending. Clearly, we should not copy the same patterns.”
Asked why she thinks the Russians do not want her to be involved in the negotiations, she says:
“They don’t want [anyone] strong on the other side because they want to push their through their maximum demands, like they have always done. Because … their tactics is very clear: at first you present threats and ultimatums, you use force, and then you will just wait, because there will always be people in the west who will offer you something you didn’t have before. And every time you go further.
So, of course, if you negotiate with anybody, you want the other side to be as weak as possible so that you can get what you want.”

Cop31 live: Climate crisis negotiations heat up on fifth day of talks
Debate over climate science, transition away from fossil fuels, electrification and climate finance can begin in earnest as world leaders leave UN summit
Real negotiations can begin as world leaders depart
Fiona Harvey
Good morning. Nearly all of the more than 90 world leaders who descended on Antalya in the past three days have now packed up their suitcases and lit out, some of them for the EU’s AI summit in Dublin. Anthony Albanese and the UN secretary-general are among the few to linger but will also head off later today.
With the departure of the circus, the real negotiations can begin, and a first draft of the cover decision for this Cop could come as soon as today, though over the weekend or Monday are still more likely. Look out for wording on the “overshoot” of 1.5C, climate science, the all-important transition away from fossil fuels, the electrification target and finance. The current “wishlist” can be perused here.
As double-hosted Cop31 gathers steam, the quest is also on for a venue for Cop33. Next year’s event will be in Ethiopia, and according to the complex systems of the 1992 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the meeting after that should be in Asia. But who will host?
As the Guardian revealed last night, it will not be China – a shame, according to many experts, who had been hoping that the world’s biggest emitter of greenhouse gases and second biggest economy would step up. China is undergoing a massive economic transformation, swapping reliance on coal and oil for electricity generated from renewable sources. This has proved a boost to the country’s economy, as the clean and low-carbon sectors now make up more than a tenth of its GDP.
India also considered hosting Cop33, but dropped its early-stage proposal months ago. That leaves the field open, with Uzbekistan, Thailand, Korea and Indonesia also cited as potential bidders. No decision on the hosting is likely to be made at this Cop, as countries are likely to need more time to develop their bids.
The race to electrification has emerged as a key theme of this year’s Cop. Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), told the Guardian yesterday that the world is now in an “age of electricity”.
But what does life look like in some of the world’s most highly electrified countries? We spoke to people in Norway, Rwanda and China to find out.
The world is now in the "age of electricity", energy agency boss says
Fiona Harvey
The world has left behind the age of coal, oil and gas and is now firmly in “the age of electricity”, the world’s leading energy economist has said.
Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), said more than twice as much electricity generation would be added to the global economy in the next decade than in the last, as countries scramble to secure their energy supplies against fossil fuel price volatility and supply shocks, such as the Iran war.
Transport is being electrified at an unprecedented rate: outside China, sales of electric cars have risen by 60% in the last nine months, the IEA has found. The growth of AI datacentres is also spurring electricity generation, as is the rapid growth in air conditioning, according to Birol, as heatwaves grow more intense and more frequent under rising global temperatures.
“We will still use oil and gas, but the dominant source of energy is becoming electricity,” Birol told the Guardian in an interview at the Cop31 UN climate summit in Turkey. “One staggering number [is that] in the last 10 years, the world has added about 5,000 gigawatts of electricity.

US House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday there was growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after a spy scandal forced out Huang, who has pushed to preserve access to the Chinese market and has close ties with US President Donald Trump.
Huang stepped down after news reports of a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.
Lawmakers from both parties have since called for tougher restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips, threatening access to chips that underpin China's surging AI development.
Senior White House officials were also discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out, two people familiar with the situation said, as the desire to take action rose across Washington.
A growing number of lawmakers have criticized Lutnick for the administration's refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a US trade blacklist, and questioned whether the government was properly overseeing Nvidia's exports to China.
Nvidia's advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.
"The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here," Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, told reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favored limiting China's access to the advanced technology. "I think there's a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take."
Investors dumped shares in Chinese AI models and hardware suppliers to the US on Friday, with AI model stocks Z.AI 2513.HK and MiniMax Group 0100.HK tumbling 12% and 8.4% respectively.
Data center suppliers Zhongji Innolight 300308.SZ and Eoptolink Technology 300502.SZ, whose businesses are heavily reliant on US markets, also slumped more than 8%.
The Chinese businesswoman at the center of the scandal, Alice Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner the US government suspects of helping China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under US export controls. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy.
REPUBLICANS EYE EXPORT RESTRICTIONS
The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions.
Reuters reported that Chinese AI companies are trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China because they are worried the Jensen Huang allegations could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on their ability to access the company's chips remotely.
Congressional Republicans are keen to attach new restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China in the annual defense authorization bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements since Monday. The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress more power over advanced AI chip exports. The Chip Security Act would require companies to track the location of advanced AI processors to prevent smuggling.
The Match Act would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China. The Remote Access Security Act would give the Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centers to access Nvidia chips.
SCRUTINY OF HUANG LIKELY TO CONTINUE
Huang's resignation is unlikely to end congressional scrutiny of Nvidia and could leave the former chief executive more exposed to investigation, said Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation.
